hooks.text: A billion-year-old star is glowing with elements that decay in decades.
One star 356 light-years away is packed with short-lived radioactive elements.
Why does a billion-year-old star shine with short-lived radioactive elements?

title: The Star That Seems To Burn Nuclear Waste
description: Astronomer Antoni Przybylski discovered a star that breaks the laws of chemistry with its strange radioactive glow.

beats.text: A billion-year-old star is glowing with elements that decay in decades.
beats.visual: Artist illustration of a magnetic star, ESO

beats.text: Our own Sun is mostly hydrogen, with heavier elements making up less than one percent of its mass.
beats.visual: Solar Dynamics Observatory ultraviolet photograph of the Sun, 2015

beats.text: Located 356 light-years away in the southern constellation Centaurus, Przybylski's Star completely flips that familiar recipe.
beats.visual: Constellation map of Centaurus showing southern sky, IAU

beats.text: In 1961, astronomer Antoni Przybylski found rare-earth metals like holmium enriched by over 1,000 times solar levels.
beats.visual: Archival photograph of astronomer Antoni Przybylski at Mount Stromlo, 1961

beats.text: Later studies reported even stranger things: short-lived radioactive elements like promethium, which decays in under 18 years.
beats.visual: Periodic table highlighting lanthanides and actinides

beats.text: That sparked wild theories of alien civilizations dumping radioactive waste inside.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a Dyson sphere or alien megastructure near a star

beats.text: But overlapping light patterns likely explain away the radioactive elements.
beats.visual: Stellar absorption spectrum showing complex Fraunhofer lines, high resolution

beats.text: Researchers are still investigating the seemingly impossible chemical makeup of this.
beats.visual: ESO 3.6-metre telescope dome at La Silla Observatory, 2020
queries: ESO La Silla Observatory night sky
